summary: Describes password-based cryptography: how to turn a human-chosen password into a cryptographic key, and how to use such keys for encryption and message authentication. It also defines the ASN.1 syntax that identifies the techniques. It is a republication of an RSA Laboratories specification. It was replaced by RFC 8018.

plainLanguage.summary: A password is easy to remember but a weak lock. This turns your short password into a strong, scrambled key, like grinding a pebble into fine sand that is hard to rebuild.

questions: how to derive a key from a password
what is a salt in password hashing
how many iterations should pbkdf2 use
subtitle: How to turn a human-chosen password into a cryptographic key, and use it for encryption and message authentication.

tldr.problem: A password is not directly usable as a key for a conventional cipher, and because passwords come from a small space, careless processing makes them easy to guess offline.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #5 v2.0 combines the password with a salt and an iteration count in a key derivation function (PBKDF1 or PBKDF2), then builds encryption schemes (PBES1, PBES2) and a message authentication scheme (PBMAC1) on top, with ASN.1 syntax to identify them.
tldr.outcome: PBKDF2 and PBES2 are recommended for new applications. The RFC is an Informational republication that has since been obsoleted by RFC 8018.

today: RFC 2898 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 8018, so that document is the current version of PKCS #5. Change control for the specification stayed with the PKCS process at RSA Laboratories.

sections.title: What PKCS #5 Covers
sections.content:
This memo is a republication of PKCS #5 v2.0 from RSA Laboratories. Change control stays with the PKCS process, and the body, except the security considerations section, is taken directly from that specification.

It gives recommendations for four things: key derivation functions, encryption schemes, message-authentication schemes, and ASN.1 syntax that identifies the techniques. They are intended for general use and are particularly aimed at protecting sensitive information such as private keys, as in PKCS #8. The RFC supersedes PKCS #5 v1.5 but includes compatible techniques.

Out of scope are other password-based techniques such as password-based entity authentication and key establishment protocols, and guidelines for choosing passwords.

The design is two-layered. A password-based key derivation function turns the password into a key. The encryption and authentication schemes then use an ordinary underlying scheme with that key, which keeps them modular.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a recipe book for turning a password into a strong secret key and then using that key to lock things. It does not tell you how to pick a good password.

sections.title: Salt and Iteration Count
sections.content:
Passwords are often chosen from a relatively small space, so the processing must defend against search attacks. Two ideas do the work. A salt is combined with the password to produce a key. It acts as an index into a large set of keys for that password and need not be secret. An iteration count makes each key derivation more expensive by repeating an underlying function many times. A modest count such as 1000 is no real burden for a legitimate party but a significant one for an opponent.

With a 64-bit salt there can be as many as 2^64 keys per password. That makes precomputing keys for a dictionary of passwords hard, and makes it unlikely that the same key is chosen twice.

The receiver cannot be sure a salt was truly random. The RFC gives an example: an opponent could replay the salt from an 80-bit key operation as if it were for a 40-bit key. So if there is no concern about interactions between uses of the same key, the salt may be random and should be at least eight octets (64 bits) long. Otherwise it should also contain data that distinguishes operations and key lengths, which the receiver checks or regenerates. For iteration count, a minimum of 1000 iterations is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The salt is a pinch of random seasoning, so two people with the same password still end up with different keys. The iteration count is how many times you stir, which is no trouble for you but makes a thief's guessing very slow.

sections.title: Key Derivation: PBKDF1 and PBKDF2
sections.content:
A password-based key derivation function takes a password P, a salt S, an iteration count c and a desired key length dkLen, and outputs a derived key DK. Two functions are specified. PBKDF2 is recommended for new applications. PBKDF1 is included only for compatibility with existing applications.

PBKDF1 applies a hash function (MD2, MD5 or SHA-1) for c iterations to the password joined with an eight-octet salt, then takes the first dkLen octets. The key length is bounded by the hash output: 16 octets for MD2 and MD5, 20 for SHA-1.

PBKDF2 uses a pseudorandom function (PRF) and can produce keys of essentially unbounded length, up to (2^32 - 1) * hLen octets. It builds the key from blocks. Each block is the exclusive-or of c chained PRF outputs. The RFC calls this a belt-and-suspenders approach: the recursion removes a degree of parallelism from an opponent and the exclusive-or reduces concerns about the recursion degenerating into a small set of values.

The example PRF is HMAC-SHA-1, with a 20-octet output. Because of how it works, the effective search space for a derived key is at most 160 bits, which the RFC says is unlikely to matter in practice for passwords.
sections.plainLanguage: PBKDF2 is a blender that mixes your password and the salt, then runs the blender again and again, and keeps adding more batches until it has made a key as long as you asked for. The older one, PBKDF1, can only make short keys.

sections.title: Encryption and Authentication Schemes
sections.content:
PBES1 combines PBKDF1 with DES or RC2 in CBC mode. It derives a 16-octet key, uses the first eight octets as the encryption key and the next eight as the initialization vector, and pads the message so its length is a multiple of eight. It is recommended only for compatibility, since its key sizes (56 or 64 bits) may not be large enough.

PBES2 combines a key derivation function, which must be PBKDF2 in this version, with an underlying encryption scheme. Steps: pick a salt and iteration count, pick the derived key length, derive the key, then encrypt. Decryption reverses this, and a decryption error is reported if the underlying scheme fails. PBES2 is recommended for new applications.

PBMAC1 is the message authentication scheme. It derives a key with PBKDF2 and then applies an underlying MAC scheme under that key. Verification recomputes the code and outputs correct or incorrect. Appendix B gives examples of supporting techniques (HMAC-SHA-1, DES-CBC-Pad, DES-EDE3-CBC-Pad, RC2-CBC-Pad and RC5-CBC-Pad) but none is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Once you have a key made from your password, you use it with a normal lock: one for hiding a message and one for proving a message was not changed. The newer versions let you choose which lock to use.

sections.title: ASN.1 Syntax and Identifiers
sections.content:
Appendix A defines ASN.1 so that applications such as PKCS #8 can say which technique was used and carry its parameters. Everything hangs off the pkcs-5 object identifier arc. For example id-PBKDF2 is {pkcs-5 12}, id-PBES2 is {pkcs-5 13} and id-PBMAC1 is {pkcs-5 14}. No identifier is given for PBKDF1; the six PBES1 identifiers (such as pbeWithSHA1AndDES-CBC, {pkcs-5 10}) cover existing uses.

The PBKDF2 parameters carry the salt, the iteration count, an optional key length and the PRF, which defaults to HMAC-SHA-1. The key length field is for convenience only and is not cryptographically protected. If different key lengths could interact for one salt, the salt should distinguish them. PBES2 and PBMAC1 parameters name a key derivation function and an underlying scheme. Appendix C repeats the syntax as a single ASN.1 module.
sections.plainLanguage: Each recipe gets a unique label number, and a small form records the seasoning and stirring count. That way whoever opens the locked box knows exactly how to rebuild the key.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that password-based cryptography is generally limited in the security it can provide, especially for methods like these where off-line password search is possible. Salt and iteration count raise the cost of attack, but it is essential that passwords are selected well and that stored passwords are protected.

In general, different keys should be derived from a password for different uses. For password-based encryption with a single algorithm, a random salt is enough to produce different keys. In other situations a structured salt is needed, as described in the salt discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a very good recipe cannot rescue a password like 1234. Pick a long, hard password and keep it safe.

data.title: PBKDF2 definition
data.code:
F (P, S, c, i) = U_1 \xor U_2 \xor ... \xor U_c

where

U_1 = PRF (P, S || INT (i)) ,
U_2 = PRF (P, U_1) ,
...
U_c = PRF (P, U_{c-1}) .

DK = T_1 || T_2 || ... || T_l<0..r-1>
